title: A Smaller, Redder Sun
sub: A cool red dwarf, half the Sun's size
blurb: Kepler-186 isn't a sun like ours — it's an M-dwarf, a small, cool star about half the Sun's size and mass that shines a dim, ember red. Stars like this are the most common in the galaxy, and they burn for far longer than our Sun ever will.

title: Caught in Transit
sub: Found by the dip in its starlight
blurb: We can't see Kepler-186's planets directly. Instead the Kepler telescope watched the star for years and caught the tiny, repeating dips in brightness as each world crossed in front of it — a fingerprint that reveals a planet's size and the length of its year.

title: The First Earth in the Zone
blurb: Kepler-186f was the first Earth-size planet ever found orbiting in its star's habitable zone — the temperate band where a rocky world could hold liquid water. Only about 10% larger than Earth, it circles at the cool outer edge of that zone.

title: A Sky of Endless Sunset
sub: Noon under a dim red sun
blurb: From the surface of Kepler-186f, the star would look bigger but far dimmer than our Sun, bathing the world in a deep red light. High noon might glow no brighter than an hour after sunset on Earth — and any plants there may have evolved darker colours to drink in the feeble red light.

title: Hidden in the Swan
blurb: Kepler-186 lies about 580 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus, the Swan. It is far too faint to see by eye — the light arriving in our telescopes tonight began its journey before the Middle Ages.
